retrievedReferences.title: The Experimental Design Assistant
retrievedReferences.titleZh: 步骤编号与反馈连接结合，区分主要操作和辅助功能。
retrievedReferences.summary:
The Experimental Design Assistant (EDA) workflow.
The workflow is not fixed and different users might prefer to do some steps in a different order. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).

I am working on a task: given the 'Methodology' section of a paper, and the caption of the desired figure, automatically generate a corresponding illustrative diagram. I will input the text of the 'Methodology' section, the figure caption, and your output should be a detailed description of an illustrative figure that effectively represents the methods described in the text.

To help you understand the task better, and grasp the principles for generating such figures, I will also provide you with several examples. You should learn from these examples to provide your figure description.

** IMPORTANT: **
Your description should be as detailed as possible. Semantically, clearly describe each element and their connections. Formally, include various details such as background style (typically pure white or very light pastel), colors, line thickness, icon styles, etc. Remember: vague or unclear specifications will only make the generated figure worse, not better.

If reference image analysis is provided, use it as structure and style guidance without copying irrelevant content. Do not include the figure title or caption text inside the image.

content.text:
Methodology Section:
Synthetic teaching example of an instrument state machine. States: Idle, Running, Paused, Completed. Initial dot enters Idle. Transitions: Idle→Running: start; Running→Paused: pause; Paused→Running: resume; Running→Completed: finish; Paused→Idle: cancel; Completed→Idle: reset. Each named state appears once. Arrows are labelled events, not process activities. Completed is not a terminal state because reset returns to Idle. English text. Reference is for structural design only.

Figure Caption:
Explicit synthetic teaching example

Detailed description of the target figure:

Retrieved 图研 reference examples for layout/style guidance:
Reference 1 (journal_pcbi.1009702.g001): Identification of periodic attractors in Boolean networks using a priori information
Example of a BN.
(A) Network structure G(V, E) for a BN consisting of n = 3 nodes x_{1}, x_{2}, and x_{3}. The Boolean functions are represented by the edges. (B) State transition diagram of all 2^{3} = 8 states of the BN represented in (A). (C) Simplification of a bBM for a phosphorylation-dephosphorylation system as elemental species-reaction graph. The nodes corresponding to elemental states of component x_{1} are shown in black, the nodes corresponding to reactions are shown with grey fillings. Here, a component (protein) x_{1} undergoes phosphorylation by consuming its elemental state x_{1}-{0} to produce its modified state x_{1}-{P} by reaction r_{1} (phosphorylation). The modified x_{1}-{P} undergoes consumption thereby producing the neutral state x_{1}-{0} via reaction r_{2} (dephosphorylation) (details in [29]). (D) Relationship between initial states of both elemental states x_{1}-{0} and x_{1}-{P} of component x_{1} and the attractors. When at least either of the two elemental states x_{1}-{0} or x_{1}-{P} are active in the initial state, both will be active in the attractor. Both elemental states need to be inactive in the initial state to be absent (inactive) in the attractor state. Both reaction nodes r_{1} and r_{2} are assumed to be active in this example and are not shown. Synthesis and degradation are not considered here. In the example, standard update rules are applied, where two mutually exclusive states can be simultaneously present. More details can be found in [29].

calls.responseText:
Based on the methodology provided and the visual style of the reference image (specifically Panel B, which depicts a state transition diagram), here is the detailed description for the illustrative figure.

**Figure Description:**

**Overall Layout and Style:**
The figure is a schematic state transition diagram presented on a pure white background. The style is clean, high-contrast, and academic, utilizing black lines and text with white-filled nodes, consistent with the reference image's Panel B. The layout arranges four main state nodes in a loose diamond or quadrilateral formation to clearly display the cyclic and branching nature of the instrument's logic.

**Nodes (States):**
There are four distinct state nodes, each represented as a rectangle with rounded corners (pill-shaped), filled with white and outlined with a solid black line (approx. 2pt thickness). Inside each node, the state name is centered in a bold, sans-serif font (e.g., Arial or Helvetica), sized for high readability.
1.  **Idle:** Located at the top-left position. This is the primary hub of the diagram.
2.  **Running:** Located at the top-right position, horizontally aligned with "Idle".
3.  **Paused:** Located at the bottom-right position, directly below "Running".
4.  **Completed:** Located at the bottom-left position, directly below "Idle" and to the left of "Paused".

**Initial State Indicator:**
A solid black circular dot (bullet point) is placed to the immediate left of the "Idle" node. A short, straight horizontal arrow connects this dot to the left edge of the "Idle" node, indicating it is the entry point of the system.

**Transitions (Edges and Labels):**
Directed connections between states are represented by solid black arrows with triangular heads. Each arrow is labeled with the specific event trigger in a smaller, regular-weight sans-serif font, placed near the midpoint of the arrow shaft.

*   **Idle $\rightarrow$ Running:** A straight horizontal arrow pointing right from "Idle" to "Running". Label: **start**.
*   **Running $\rightarrow$ Paused:** A straight vertical arrow pointing down from "Running" to "Paused". Label: **pause**.
*   **Paused $\rightarrow$ Running:** A straight vertical arrow pointing up from "Paused" to "Running" (parallel to the 'pause' arrow but slightly offset or curved to avoid overlap if necessary, though straight parallel lines are acceptable if spaced well). Label: **resume**.
*   **Running $\rightarrow$ Completed:** A long, curved arrow arching over the top or sweeping underneath from "Running" to "Completed". Alternatively, a diagonal arrow crossing the center. Given the layout, a curved arrow sweeping under "Paused" or over the top connecting "Running" to "Completed" is clearest. Let's specify a curved arrow sweeping underneath the diagram from "Running" to "Completed" to avoid crossing the vertical loop. Label: **finish**.
*   **Paused $\rightarrow$ Idle:** A long, curved arrow sweeping along the bottom or side from "Paused" back to "Idle". To distinguish from the "finish" arrow, this can sweep along the outer bottom edge. Label: **cancel**.
*   **Completed $\rightarrow$ Idle:** A straight vertical arrow pointing up from "Completed" to "Idle". Label: **reset**.

**Visual Logic Check:**
*   The diagram explicitly shows that "Completed" is not a terminal state because of the upward "reset" arrow returning to "Idle".
*   All labels correspond strictly to the events provided (start, pause, resume, finish, cancel, reset).
*   No process activities are listed on the arrows, only triggers.

job.methodContent: Synthetic teaching example of an instrument state machine. States: Idle, Running, Paused, Completed. Initial dot enters Idle. Transitions: Idle→Running: start; Running→Paused: pause; Paused→Running: resume; Running→Completed: finish; Paused→Idle: cancel; Completed→Idle: reset. Each named state appears once. Arrows are labelled events, not process activities. Completed is not a terminal state because reset returns to Idle. English text. Reference is for structural design only.

retrievedReferences.titleZh: 同一布尔网络分别呈现实体连接、全状态转移、反应机制及真值表，展示节点语义随图型改变。
retrievedReferences.summary:
Example of a BN.
(A) Network structure G(V, E) for a BN consisting of n = 3 nodes x_{1}, x_{2}, and x_{3}. The Boolean functions are represented by the edges. (B) State transition diagram of all 2^{3} = 8 states of the BN represented in (A). (C) Simplification of a bBM for a phosphorylation-dephosphorylation system as elemental species-reaction graph. The nodes corresponding to elemental states of component x_{1} are shown in black, the nodes corresponding to reactions are shown with grey fillings. Here, a component (protein) x_{1} undergoes phosphorylation by consuming its elemental state x_{1}-{0} to produce its modified state x_{1}-{P} by reaction r_{1} (phosphorylation). The modified x_{1}-{P} undergoes consumption thereby producing the neutral state x_{1}-{0} via reaction r_{2} (dephosphorylation) (details in [29]). (D) Relationship between initial states of both elemental states x_{1}-{0} and x_{1}-{P} of component x_{1} and the attractors. When at least either of the two elemental states x_{1}-{0} or x_{1}-{P} are active in the initial state, both will be active in the attractor. Both elemental states need to be inactive in the initial state to be absent (inactive) in the attractor state. Both reaction nodes r_{1} and r_{2} are assumed to be active in this example and are not shown. Synthesis and degradation are not considered here. In the example, standard update rules are applied, where two mutually exclusive states can be simultaneously present. More details can be found in [29].

stages.title: 规划
stages.text:
Based on the methodology provided and the visual style of the reference image (specifically Panel B, which depicts a state transition diagram), here is the detailed description for the illustrative figure.

**Figure Description:**

**Overall Layout and Style:**
The figure is a schematic state transition diagram presented on a pure white background. The style is clean, high-contrast, and academic, utilizing black lines and text with white-filled nodes, consistent with the reference image's Panel B. The layout arranges four main state nodes in a loose diamond or quadrilateral formation to clearly display the cyclic and branching nature of the instrument's logic.

**Nodes (States):**
There are four distinct state nodes, each represented as a rectangle with rounded corners (pill-shaped), filled with white and outlined with a solid black line (approx. 2pt thickness). Inside each node, the state name is centered in a bold, sans-serif font (e.g., Arial or Helvetica), sized for high readability.
1.  **Idle:** Located at the top-left position. This is the primary hub of the diagram.
2.  **Running:** Located at the top-right position, horizontally aligned with "Idle".
3.  **Paused:** Located at the bottom-right position, directly below "Running".
4.  **Completed:** Located at the bottom-left position, directly below "Idle" and to the left of "Paused".

**Initial State Indicator:**
A solid black circular dot (bullet point) is placed to the immediate left of the "Idle" node. A short, straight horizontal arrow connects this dot to the left edge of the "Idle" node, indicating it is the entry point of the system.

**Transitions (Edges and Labels):**
Directed connections between states are represented by solid black arrows with triangular heads. Each arrow is labeled with the specific event trigger in a smaller, regular-weight sans-serif font, placed near the midpoint of the arrow shaft.

*   **Idle $\rightarrow$ Running:** A straight horizontal arrow pointing right from "Idle" to "Running". Label: **start**.
*   **Running $\rightarrow$ Paused:** A straight vertical arrow pointing down from "Running" to "Paused". Label: **pause**.
*   **Paused $\rightarrow$ Running:** A straight vertical arrow pointing up from "Paused" to "Running" (parallel to the 'pause' arrow but slightly offset or curved to avoid overlap if necessary, though straight parallel lines are acceptable if spaced well). Label: **resume**.
*   **Running $\rightarrow$ Completed:** A long, curved arrow arching over the top or sweeping underneath from "Running" to "Completed". Alternatively, a diagonal arrow crossing the center. Given the layout, a curved arrow sweeping under "Paused" or over the top connecting "Running" to "Completed" is clearest. Let's specify a curved arrow sweeping underneath the diagram from "Running" to "Completed" to avoid crossing the vertical loop. Label: **finish**.
*   **Paused $\rightarrow$ Idle:** A long, curved arrow sweeping along the bottom or side from "Paused" back to "Idle". To distinguish from the "finish" arrow, this can sweep along the outer bottom edge. Label: **cancel**.
*   **Completed $\rightarrow$ Idle:** A straight vertical arrow pointing up from "Completed" to "Idle". Label: **reset**.

**Visual Logic Check:**
*   The diagram explicitly shows that "Completed" is not a terminal state because of the upward "reset" arrow returning to "Idle".
*   All labels correspond strictly to the events provided (start, pause, resume, finish, cancel, reset).
*   No process activities are listed on the arrows, only triggers.

Methodology Section:
Synthetic teaching example, not a research result. Draw exactly Start → Receive sample → Quality check (diamond). Label yes branch → Normalize → Output → End. Label no branch → Reject sample → End. Use English text. Distinguish operations from decisions and start/end. No numeric or scientific claims. Reference image is for design structure only; do not transfer its paper data or conclusions.

Figure Caption:
Synthetic sample process

Detailed description of the target figure:

Retrieved 图研 reference examples for layout/style guidance:
Reference 1 (journal_pbio.2003779.g001): The Experimental Design Assistant
The Experimental Design Assistant (EDA) workflow.
The workflow is not fixed and different users might prefer to do some steps in a different order. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).

Based on the methodology provided and the visual style of the reference image (teal/green palette, white icons/text, clean flat design), here is the detailed description for the illustrative figure.

**Figure Description:**

**Overall Layout and Style:**
The image is a vertical flowchart diagram set against a pure white background. The visual style mimics the reference image: it uses a distinct teal-green color (approximate hex #1F8A70) for process blocks and decision points, with white text and icons. The flow moves from top to bottom. All shapes have sharp corners or standard geometric angles (no rounded "pill" shapes for start/end, strictly following flowchart conventions). Connecting lines are solid black arrows with standard triangular heads, 2px thickness.

**Elements and Flow (Top to Bottom):**

1.  **Start Node:**
    *   **Shape:** A stadium shape (rectangle with semi-circular ends), filled with the primary teal-green color.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Start"**.
    *   **Position:** Top center of the canvas.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the next block.

2.  **Process Block 1 (Receive Sample):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Width is approximately 30% of the canvas width.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Receive sample"**. To the left of the text, include a simple white line-art icon of a test tube or beaker to match the scientific theme of the reference style.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the decision diamond.

3.  **Decision Node (Quality Check):**
    *   **Shape:** A diamond (rhombus) shape, filled with teal-green. The width matches the rectangular blocks above.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Quality check"**.
    *   **Connections (Branching):**
        *   **Yes Branch:** An arrow exits from the **bottom** vertex of the diamond, pointing vertically down. A small label **"Yes"** in black text is placed next to the arrow shaft.
        *   **No Branch:** An arrow exits from the **right** vertex of the diamond, travels horizontally to the right, then turns 90 degrees downward. A small label **"No"** in black text is placed next to the horizontal segment.

4.  **Process Block 2 (Normalize - Yes Path):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Aligned directly below the Decision Node.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Normalize"**. Include a white line-art icon of a graph or slider to represent adjustment/normalization.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the Output block.

5.  **Process Block 3 (Output - Yes Path):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Aligned directly below the "Normalize" block.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Output"**. Include a white line-art icon of a document or a tray.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the End node.

6.  **Process Block 4 (Reject Sample - No Path):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Positioned to the right of the main vertical axis, aligned horizontally with the "Normalize" block.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Reject sample"**. Include a white line-art icon of a trash bin or an "X" mark.
    *   **Connection:** An arrow exits the bottom of this block, travels down, then turns 90 degrees to the left to merge into the final "End" node (or simply points to a separate End node if preferred, but merging is cleaner). *Alternative simpler layout:* The arrow points down to its own specific "End" terminator located below it. Let's use the specific terminator approach for clarity.

7.  **End Nodes:**
    *   **Shape:** Stadium shapes (identical to the Start node), filled with teal-green.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"End"**.
    *   **Positions:**
        *   One "End" node is located at the very bottom of the central column (connected from "Output").
        *   One "End" node is located at the bottom of the right-hand column (connected from "Reject sample").

**Typography and Colors:**
*   **Font:** Sans-serif (e.g., Arial, Helvetica, or Noto Sans), bold weight for legibility.
*   **Text Color:** Pure White (#FFFFFF) inside the teal blocks; Black (#000000) for branch labels ("Yes", "No") on the white background.
*   **Block Color:** Teal Green (matching reference, approx #1F8A70).
*   **Arrow Color:** Black (#000000).
*   **Background:** Pure White (#FFFFFF).

**Summary of Visual Logic:**
The diagram clearly distinguishes the linear success path (Start -> Receive -> Check -> Yes -> Normalize -> Output -> End) from the failure path (Check -> No -> Reject -> End) using spatial separation (vertical vs. side branch) and standard flowchart geometry (diamonds for decisions, rectangles for actions).

The Experimental Design Assistant (EDA) workflow.
The workflow is not fixed and different users might prefer to do some steps in a different order. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).

(6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. retrievedReferences.title: The Experimental Design Assistant
retrievedReferences.titleZh: 步骤编号与反馈连接结合，区分主要操作和辅助功能。
retrievedReferences.summary:
The Experimental Design Assistant (EDA) workflow.
The workflow is not fixed and different users might prefer to do some steps in a different order. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).

stages.title: 面板 A · 规划
stages.text:
Based on the methodology provided and the visual style of the reference image (teal/green palette, white icons/text, clean flat design), here is the detailed description for the illustrative figure.

**Figure Description:**

**Overall Layout and Style:**
The image is a vertical flowchart diagram set against a pure white background. The visual style mimics the reference image: it uses a distinct teal-green color (approximate hex #1F8A70) for process blocks and decision points, with white text and icons. The flow moves from top to bottom. All shapes have sharp corners or standard geometric angles (no rounded "pill" shapes for start/end, strictly following flowchart conventions). Connecting lines are solid black arrows with standard triangular heads, 2px thickness.

**Elements and Flow (Top to Bottom):**

1.  **Start Node:**
    *   **Shape:** A stadium shape (rectangle with semi-circular ends), filled with the primary teal-green color.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Start"**.
    *   **Position:** Top center of the canvas.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the next block.

2.  **Process Block 1 (Receive Sample):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Width is approximately 30% of the canvas width.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Receive sample"**. To the left of the text, include a simple white line-art icon of a test tube or beaker to match the scientific theme of the reference style.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the decision diamond.

3.  **Decision Node (Quality Check):**
    *   **Shape:** A diamond (rhombus) shape, filled with teal-green. The width matches the rectangular blocks above.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Quality check"**.
    *   **Connections (Branching):**
        *   **Yes Branch:** An arrow exits from the **bottom** vertex of the diamond, pointing vertically down. A small label **"Yes"** in black text is placed next to the arrow shaft.
        *   **No Branch:** An arrow exits from the **right** vertex of the diamond, travels horizontally to the right, then turns 90 degrees downward. A small label **"No"** in black text is placed next to the horizontal segment.

4.  **Process Block 2 (Normalize - Yes Path):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Aligned directly below the Decision Node.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Normalize"**. Include a white line-art icon of a graph or slider to represent adjustment/normalization.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the Output block.

5.  **Process Block 3 (Output - Yes Path):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Aligned directly below the "Normalize" block.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Output"**. Include a white line-art icon of a document or a tray.
    *   **Connection:** A straight black arrow points vertically downward to the End node.

6.  **Process Block 4 (Reject Sample - No Path):**
    *   **Shape:** A standard rectangle with sharp corners, filled with teal-green. Positioned to the right of the main vertical axis, aligned horizontally with the "Normalize" block.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"Reject sample"**. Include a white line-art icon of a trash bin or an "X" mark.
    *   **Connection:** An arrow exits the bottom of this block, travels down, then turns 90 degrees to the left to merge into the final "End" node (or simply points to a separate End node if preferred, but merging is cleaner). *Alternative simpler layout:* The arrow points down to its own specific "End" terminator located below it. Let's use the specific terminator approach for clarity.

7.  **End Nodes:**
    *   **Shape:** Stadium shapes (identical to the Start node), filled with teal-green.
    *   **Content:** Centered white text reading **"End"**.
    *   **Positions:**
        *   One "End" node is located at the very bottom of the central column (connected from "Output").
        *   One "End" node is located at the bottom of the right-hand column (connected from "Reject sample").

**Typography and Colors:**
*   **Font:** Sans-serif (e.g., Arial, Helvetica, or Noto Sans), bold weight for legibility.
*   **Text Color:** Pure White (#FFFFFF) inside the teal blocks; Black (#000000) for branch labels ("Yes", "No") on the white background.
*   **Block Color:** Teal Green (matching reference, approx #1F8A70).
*   **Arrow Color:** Black (#000000).
*   **Background:** Pure White (#FFFFFF).

**Summary of Visual Logic:**
The diagram clearly distinguishes the linear success path (Start -> Receive -> Check -> Yes -> Normalize -> Output -> End) from the failure path (Check -> No -> Reject -> End) using spatial separation (vertical vs. side branch) and standard flowchart geometry (diamonds for decisions, rectangles for actions).

The Experimental Design Assistant (EDA) workflow.
The workflow is not fixed and different users might prefer to do some steps in a different order. A potential workflow using the different functionalities of the EDA is described as follows: (1) The user starts by drawing a diagram (with nodes and links) representing the experiment they are planning. Assistance is provided in the form of examples, templates, and video tutorials. (2) Information is added into the node properties, providing more details about the specific step of the process represented by each node. (3) The “Critique” functionality (see Table 2) enables the researcher to obtain feedback on the diagram and the design it represents. The feedback might prompt a change in their plans or the addition of missing information. This is an iterative process and the user might go through the first 3 steps a number of times. (4) Once feedback from the critique has been addressed and the user is satisfied with the final design, the analysis method suggested by the system can be reviewed (see Table 2). (5) Depending on how the data will be analysed, a suitable sample size can be calculated using one of the calculators provided within the system. (6) Once the number of animals needed per group is known, the EDA can generate the randomisation sequence. The spreadsheet detailing the group allocation for each animal can be sent directly to a third party nominated by the user, thus blinding the allocation. This enables the researcher to remain unaware of the group allocation until the data have been collected and analysed. (7) Diagrams can be safely shared with colleagues and collaborators at any stage of the process. (8) The user can export a PDF report, which contains key information about the internal validity of the experiment, a summary of the feedback from the system, and the EDA diagram itself. This report can be submitted as part of a grant application, as part of the ethical review process, or, later on, with a journal manuscript. Alternatively, the diagram data can be exported (as an.eda file) and saved locally or used to register the protocol before the experiment is conducted. (9) Once the planning is complete, the experiment is carried out. (10) The diagram can be updated after data collection to enable the user to keep an accurate record (e.g., to record the number of animals analysed if some failed to complete the experiment or if data are missing for other reasons).
